name: Updating Two-Dimensional List (Case 2)
description: Construct a program that initializes a 3x3 two-dimensional matrix that has the numbers 1 through 9 for entries, updates the middle row to a list filled with 1s, then sets the top-right element of the matrix to be 10, and finally prints the matrix.
code:
#Step 1: Define a 3x3 two-dimensional list 
matrix = [[ 1, 2, 3 ],
          [ 4, 5, 6 ],
          [ 7, 8, 9 ]]
#Step 2: Update the two-dimensional list 
matrix[1] = [1, 1, 1]
matrix[0][2] = 10
#Step 3: Print the list
print(matrix)

commentList: Purpose: This line starts the assignment of a 3x3 two-dimensional list to the variable matrix — you are creating the first row [1, 2, 3] and beginning the outer list that will hold all three rows.

Syntax breakdown: matrix is the variable name, = assigns a value, the first [ opens the outer list, the second [ opens the first inner list (the first row), the numbers 1, 2, 3 are integer literals separated by commas, the ] closes that inner list, and the trailing comma separates this row from the next row that follows on the next line.

Semantics: After this line (together with the following lines that complete the literal), matrix will be a list of lists where each inner list represents a row. You will later refer to rows as matrix[0], matrix[1], etc., and to elements as matrix[row][col].

Potential errors and misconceptions: If you forget the comma after an element or after the inner list, or you forget a closing ], Python will raise a SyntaxError. Also, this is just nested Python lists, not a special 'matrix' object — operations on nested lists behave like normal lists.

Common pitfall: Some learners try to make identical rows with multiplication like [[1,1,1]]*3; that creates three references to the same inner list so changing one row would change them all. Here you avoid that by writing each row explicitly.

How it contributes to the solution: This line provides the initial data you will modify — the later lines replace the middle row and change the top-right element, so you need this concrete layout to show those updates.

Best practices: Use a clear, descriptive name like matrix, keep consistent spacing and commas for readability, and for larger or generated matrices consider using list comprehensions or loops instead of writing every row by hand so your code scales better.

commentList: Purpose: You replace the entire middle row of the 3x3 matrix with a new row of three 1s, so the second row becomes [1, 1, 1] and the program meets the requirement to update the middle row.

Syntax and semantics: matrix[1] selects the second sublist (because indexing starts at 0). The = operator assigns a new list literal [1, 1, 1] to that position, so the whole sublist at index 1 is replaced rather than changing a single element.

Indexing note: Because Python lists are zero-indexed, matrix[0] is the first row, matrix[1] is the middle row, and matrix[2] is the last row. If you used an index outside 0..2 you'd get an IndexError.

Common misconceptions and pitfalls: If you assign the same list object to multiple rows (for example by doing shared = [1,1,1]; matrix[1] = shared; matrix[2] = shared), then modifying one row later will also change the other, because they refer to the same list. Also make sure the new row has the correct number of columns (3) to avoid uneven row lengths.

Best practices: Use an explicit list literal like [1, 1, 1] for clarity and to create an independent row. If you only want to change one element, assign to matrix[1][col_index] instead. If you must copy a list for multiple rows, create separate copies (e.g., list([...]) or a comprehension) so rows remain independent.

commentList: Purpose: This line sets the top-right element of the matrix to 10. You are changing the value in the first row (row index 0) and third column (column index 2) so that matrix[0][2] becomes 10.

Syntax and semantics: matrix[0] selects the first row (a list), and [2] selects the third item in that row. The = 10 is an assignment that replaces the existing value (3) with 10. You are mutating the existing two-dimensional list in place.

Potential errors and misconceptions: Remember Python uses zero-based indexing, so the top-right item is [0][2], not [1][3]. If an index is out of range you'll get IndexError (for example, using [0][3]). If matrix[0] were a tuple instead of a list, trying to assign would raise a TypeError because tuples are immutable.

Best practices: Use clear comments or named variables for row/column indices if you refer to them often (e.g., row = 0; col = 2; matrix[row][col] = 10). You can also check the matrix shape with len(matrix) and len(matrix[0]) before assigning to avoid index errors, and print or test after the change to confirm you updated the intended element.

commentList: Purpose: This line sends the current value of matrix to the console so you can see the final 3x3 list after the updates.
Syntax: print(matrix) calls Python's print function with one argument (the variable matrix). The function converts the matrix to text and writes that text to standard output.
What you will see: because matrix is a nested list, Python prints its list representation; after the given changes you should see something like [[1, 2, 10], [1, 1, 1], [7, 8, 9]].

Common misconceptions/errors: in Python 3 you must use parentheses—writing print matrix (without ()) is a syntax error. Also, print(matrix) only displays the current contents; it does not change the matrix or create a copy.
Formatting note: print(matrix) shows the whole nested list on one line. If you want each row on its own line for readability, you can do: for row in matrix: print(row) or print(*matrix, sep='\n').

Best practice: when printing data for users, add a short label (for example print('Matrix:', matrix)) or use the pprint module to make complex structures easier to read; avoid printing very large structures in production code.

distractors.description: Choosing matrix[2] = [1, 1, 1] suggests you think the third index is the middle row. If you run this line, you replace the last row with three 1s, so the matrix becomes [ [1,2,3], [4,5,6], [1,1,1] ]. The program will still execute and print, but you have updated the wrong row: the bottom row was changed instead of the intended middle row. This is a classic off-by-one indexing mistake — you are using the wrong row index, so the matrix does not reflect the required modification to the middle row.

[backfilled] Choosing this line typically comes from thinking columns are numbered 1..3 (so you use 3 for the third column) or otherwise miscounting positions. In Python, a row with three elements has valid column indices 0, 1, 2, so trying to access index 3 will raise an IndexError at runtime and crash the program before it prints anything. Because this line attempts to access an element that doesn't exist, it is invalid for the given matrix size and will prevent the program from completing successfully.

If you write this line, you will change a different element in the matrix (the element in the last row, first column) rather than the one the task intends to update. You might pick this because you mix up the order of indices and think the first number selects a column or you imagine coordinates with the origin at the bottom. The program will still run and print a matrix, but the wrong entry will become 10 and the output will not match the requirement. This line is incorrect because it targets a different position in the nested lists — it does not address the specific element you need to change.

[backfilled] If you write matrix[1] = 1 you may be assuming that giving one value for a row will automatically fill all positions in that row with that value. Step by step, this line replaces the entire second entry of the outer list with the integer 1, so the matrix becomes something like [ [1,2,3], 1, [7,8,9] ]. You would still be able to print the outer list, but the middle row is no longer a list of three items — it's a single integer. That breaks the intended matrix structure and any later code that expects to index into the middle row (for example, matrix[1][0]) will fail. The core problem is that a scalar value is not a list of repeated elements; the distractor incorrectly uses a single integer where a sequence of three integers is required.

[backfilled] Using matrix[1] = (1, 1, 1) replaces the second row with a tuple instead of a list. You might pick this because tuples and lists look similar and both hold multiple values. After this assignment the matrix will contain a tuple in that row (for example [ [1,2,3], (1,1,1), [7,8,9] ]). While printing still works, the middle row is not a list of ones and is immutable, so later code that expects to modify that row or relies on list-specific behavior could fail. The mistake is treating a tuple as an equivalent replacement for a list when the requirement is specifically a list of ones.

In Python, however, '==' is a comparison operator: it checks whether the element equals 10 and returns True or False, but it does not change the matrix. If you use this line, the program will run without error, but the matrix will remain unchanged and the output will not reflect the intended update.
